# create_html_artifact — one-pager output

## Purpose
This tool exists for exactly one job, and it is a narrow one: producing a static overview or summary of a larger, already-completed body of work, packaged as a shareable one-pager. Good examples of what belongs here: a finished report summarizing findings, a wrap-up of a multi-step task the user just finished with you, a consolidated view of results gathered across a conversation, or a polished recap someone could forward to a colleague without further editing. This is not a general-purpose "make it look nicer" formatter, and it is not a way to make any output feel more finished — most of what you produce in a conversation, including long or well-organized answers, should still just be a normal chat reply. Three rules make this concrete:
1. Only for an overview or summary of a completed body of work. If the content you're about to generate is itself the primary deliverable — a single answer to a question, one example, one explanation — it does not qualify, even if it's long, even if it's detailed, and even if formatting it as a page would look good. Ask yourself: "is this a recap of work already done, or is this the work itself?" If it's the work itself, this tool is the wrong choice.
2. Static content only, with no exceptions. <script> tags and all inline event handlers are stripped automatically when the artifact is saved, so nothing you produce through this tool can ever actually be interactive, no matter how it's written — buttons won't click, forms won't submit, calculators won't calculate. If the user is asking for something that needs to actually work — an app, a calculator, a live dashboard, anything with real behavior — this tool cannot deliver that and you should use file generation instead, not this tool.
3. Never a substitute for a code snippet or a mermaid diagram, even when the underlying content happens to be HTML or CSS. If what the user actually wants is a code example, a template, a demonstration of how something is built, or a diagram of a flow or architecture, the right home for that is a fenced code block or a mermaid diagram directly in your chat reply — not this tool, even if you could technically wrap that same content in an HTML page.
When you're not sure whether a given request matches this purpose, the safe default is to not call this tool and just reply inline instead. It is far better to under-use this tool than to over-use it.

## Do NOT use this tool for
- Short answers, or anything that would read naturally as a normal inline chat reply — if it would work fine as regular text, leave it as regular text.
- Code snippets, examples, templates, tutorials, or demonstrations of how to build something — this holds true even if the output would technically be a full, well-structured HTML page.
- Diagrams, flows, architecture sketches, or anything that is fundamentally a diagram rather than a document — use a mermaid code block for these instead.
- Anything interactive: forms, calculators, small apps, live dashboards, or any UI element that implies the user will click, type, or interact with it and expect a real response. Remember: this tool cannot produce working interactivity under any circumstances.

## When you do call this tool
- The tool call must be the last action you take in the turn — do not add more content after it. Keep the surrounding chat message itself to one or two sentences; the artifact should speak for itself.
- Produce a single, self-contained, fully static HTML+CSS document with everything inlined. Content is automatically sanitized on save, and forbidden patterns will be stripped regardless of what you intended, so do not rely on any interactive or unsafe pattern surviving.
- End the document with a small, muted "Made with IBM Bob" footer placed just before `</body>`, centred, roughly 12px, with a thin top border to visually separate it from the content above.
- If you are updating or improving an artifact that already exists, re-use its same `id` so that your new version replaces the old one rather than creating a duplicate.

## Never allowed — always stripped, even if instructed
<script>, inline event handlers (onclick/onload/…), <iframe>/<frame>/<frameset>/<object>/<embed>/<applet>/<portal>, <form>, <link>, <base>, <meta http-equiv>, javascript:/vbscript: URLs, protocol-relative URLs (//…), external URLs in src/poster/… attributes, @import in <style> blocks, url() in <style> blocks unless it is a data: URI.
<a href> to external sites is fine. Inline data: image URIs are fine.

## Design
Single column, max-width ~760px, centred. No animations, gradients, shadows, emojis, or decorative icons. SVG only for data visualisation.
Font: `-apple-system, "Segoe UI", system-ui, sans-serif`, ~14–15px, line-height ~1.6.
Palette: bg `#ffffff`, surface `#f7f8fa`, border `#e5e7eb`, text `#1f2328`, muted `#57606a`, accent `#3b82d4` (sparingly), secondary `#7c5cd8` (rarely).

# Mode Switching

You can switch between different modes using the switch_mode tool. Each mode provides access to different capabilities and tools optimized for specific types of tasks.

Only switch modes when the user explicitly asks you to or the current mode lacks a capability required to complete the request. Do not switch modes merely because the user asks a question.

# glob — file search
Use `glob` to find files by name pattern (e.g. "**/*.ts", "src/**/*.test.ts"). Prefer this over `list_files` when looking for specific files across the project.
Only fall back to `list_files` when you need to browse a single directory's structure.

# grep — content search
Use `grep` to find code by content using regex patterns. Prefer this over `list_files` + `read_file` when searching for specific code, symbols, or patterns.
Use `read_file` only after grep tells you which file and lines to look at.

# Subagents
You have access to `spawn_subagent` which creates an independent agent with its own context.

**Default: do the work yourself.** Most tasks are faster and cheaper without a subagent.
Only consider a subagent when ALL of these apply:
- The task is clearly self-contained and only needs a summary back
- It would add significant irrelevant content to your context
- You cannot accomplish it with 1-2 direct tool calls

Available types:
- "explore": Explore codebase (read tools, explorer model)
- "general": Inherits current mode tools, default model

**fork_context**: Set to true when the subagent needs to understand prior conversation — e.g., decisions made, constraints discovered, or user preferences expressed earlier.
Leave false (default) when the description alone is sufficient context.

Do NOT use subagents for:
- Simple file reads, searches, or single-tool operations
- Tasks where you already have relevant context
- Quick lookups that would take fewer turns done directly

# create_chart — chart output
Use the `create_chart` tool when the user asks for a chart or data visualisation.

## How it works
Call the tool with:
- `type`: one of LineChart | BarChart | PieChart | ScatterChart | RadarChart | BoxplotChart
- `title`: short human-readable title for the chart tile
- `props`: a JSON string of chart-specific props

The props JSON must be valid for the chosen chart type. Do NOT wrap it in a spec fence.
Example for BarChart:
{"xAxisData":["Jan","Feb","Mar"],"series":[{"name":"Revenue","data":[4200,5800,3900]}],"title":"Monthly Revenue"}

Activate the `create-chart` skill before building props to get the full per-type prop schemas.

14 | ## The workflow this fixes: release and application-maintenance paperwork
15 | 
16 | Every production change — a release, a config update, a patch, a runbook edit — drags a paper trail behind it: the design doc, the change-approval sign-off, the test evidence, the audit log of who touched what and when. In most engineering organizations that trail lives in **five different places at once** — a FileNet or SharePoint repository for "official" documents, a shared drive for working copies, email threads for approvals, a spreadsheet for the audit tracker, and, for the unlucky few, a mainframe-attached DMS nobody wants to touch. When a release goes wrong or an auditor asks "who approved this change and where's the proof," the honest answer is usually: *it takes hours to reconstruct, across systems that don't talk to each other.*
17 | 
18 | That reconstruction tax is the specific developer-adjacent workflow C-ECM targets — **application maintenance and release/deployment governance** — and it is measurable: manual cross-system search during an incident, duplicate/near-duplicate runbook versions because nobody can tell which copy is current, approval sign-offs that exist only as an email nobody can produce six months later, and compliance audits that turn into a week-long archaeology dig instead of a five-minute report pull.
19 | 
20 | **C-ECM removes the tax without a migration.** It's a governance layer that sits *in front of* whatever storage each team already uses — IBM FileNet, an IBM i or IBM Z shop, SharePoint, Google Drive, Box, S3, Azure Blob — and gives every one of those systems the same approval gates, the same audit trail, and the same cross-repository search, on day one, with zero files moved.
21 | 
22 | **Who this is for:** release/change managers running a CAB-style sign-off process, platform and DevOps engineers who own the runbooks and deployment checklists, and IT compliance/audit teams who need to answer "prove it" requests in minutes rather than days. They interact with it exactly like a shared drive — browse, open, comment — but every one of those actions is now approval-gated, versioned, and audit-logged behind the scenes, across every backend at once, not just the newest one.
23 | 
24 | ---
25 | 
26 | ## Architecture
27 | 
28 | ```
29 | ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
30 | │                C-ECM UI (React 19 + TypeScript)       │
31 | └───────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
32 |                         │  REST API  (FastAPI · Python 3.12)
33 | ┌───────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────┐
34 | │          Provider Abstraction Layer (Strategy)        │
35 | └─┬────┬────┬─────┬──────┬────┬────┬────┬────┬────┬────┘
36 |   │    │    │     │      │    │    │    │    │    │
37 | FileNet IBM-i IBM-Z Alfresco Google OneDrive Box S3 Azure/COS Local
38 | ```
39 | 
40 | Every write to any backend — upload, rename, delete, approval vote, restore — flows through one **event bus** (`activity_service`) that fans out synchronously to the audit log, in-app notifications, and outbound webhooks. That single choke point is what makes a unified audit trail possible across 11 unrelated storage systems: no provider has to know the audit log exists, and no new provider needs new audit code.
41 | 
42 | **Design patterns in play:**
43 | - **Strategy / Adapter** — `StorageProvider` ABC with 11 concrete backends, each implementing the same interface (list, upload, download, search, versions) regardless of how alien the underlying system is (an IBM Z mainframe and Google Drive look identical to the rest of the app)
44 | - **Observer / Event Bus** — one `record_event()` call reaches audit, notifications, and webhooks; adding a new subscriber never touches provider code
45 | - **Repository** — one store module per domain (documents, workflows, tags, retention, …); routers never write raw SQL
46 | - **State Machine** — approval-workflow instances move through validated transitions only (`in_review → approved | rejected | cancelled`), with per-step vote quorum
47 | - **Factory / Registry** — `get_provider(key)` self-registers every backend; verified thread-safe under concurrent first access (see Engineering rigor, below)
48 | - **Layered Architecture** — Presentation → API → Domain → Data → Providers, so a UI or storage-backend change never leaks into the other
49 | 
50 | ---
51 | 
52 | ## Feature set
53 | 
54 | | Feature | Description |
55 | |---------|-------------|
56 | | **11 Storage Backends, One Governance Layer** | FileNet, IBM i (AS/400), IBM Z (mainframe), Alfresco, Google Drive, OneDrive/SharePoint, Box, AWS S3, Azure Blob, IBM Cloud Object Storage, Local Disk — zero migration required |
57 | | **Approval Workflows** | Multi-step, multi-reviewer, quorum-based sign-off with full history — act inline from a document's own viewer, the same gate a release or change-management process needs |
58 | | **Workflow Designer** | Admin UI to build step-based approval definitions, reviewers picked from real accounts, not free-text names |
59 | | **Audit Trail & Compliance Reporting** | Every login, view, edit, approval, and deletion logged; a 360° admin dashboard with date/user/event-category filters, trend and breakdown charts, a most-active-users ranking, automatic alerts on failed-login or bulk-delete bursts, and one-click CSV export for an auditor |
60 | | **Cross-Backend Global Search** | Every configured backend queried in parallel, latency bounded by the slowest single connection (not the sum of them), errors isolated per-connection so one bad backend never hides the rest of your results |
61 | | **Unified Document Viewer** | One full-screen view per file — properties, approvals, AI insights, tags, comments, version history, share links, and actions, each independently collapsible and lazily loaded |
62 | | **Version History & Check-Out/In** | Full version tracking with restore, and a server-enforced soft-lock (HTTP 423) so two people can't silently overwrite each other's edit to the same runbook |
63 | | **Retention Policies & Legal Hold** | Scheduled retention rules that follow a document across its lifecycle — the record survives even if the file gets moved or renamed |
64 | | **Multi-User RBAC** | Admin / Editor / Viewer roles with JWT auth and server-side session logout, audited like everything else |
65 | | **Outbound Webhooks** | HMAC-SHA256 signed, SSRF-hardened event delivery so external systems (a ticketing tool, a SIEM) hear about a change the moment it happens |
66 | | **AI Document Intelligence** | Summarize, classify, and answer questions about any document via IBM watsonx.ai / Watson NLU / Watson Discovery (OpenAI or local Ollama also supported) |
67 | | **E-Signature** | Route documents through DocuSign for a formal, legally-binding sign-off, tracked alongside every other event on that document |
68 | | **PWA / Mobile-Responsive** | Installable, usable from a phone during an on-call incident, not just a desk |
69 | 
70 | ---
71 | 
72 | ## Built with IBM Bob 2.0 — agentic development, not autocomplete
73 | 
74 | This project's entire build — from the first storage adapter to the last concurrency bug fix — was carried out through IBM Bob 2.0 operating in **Agent mode**, not as a line-completion assistant. Concretely, across the build:
75 | 
76 | - **Document understanding, applied to the hackathon itself.** Bob read all three official hackathon PDFs (the Compete page, the theme/judging page, and the Official Rules) directly, and used them to re-scope and rewrite this README against the actual theme and judging criteria — the same document-understanding capability the theme asks the *submission* to demonstrate, used here on the submission process itself.
77 | - **Parallel subagents for code review.** A single review pass fanned out 8 parallel subagents across the codebase — conventions, simplification opportunities, dead code, efficiency, and line-by-line correctness — each returning independent findings that were then triaged and fixed, rather than one linear pass.
78 | - **Multi-step, autonomous debugging.** Global Search was reported broken; Bob didn't stop at the first bug. It traced the issue through three independent layers in one session — a frontend navigation bug, a backend schema/serialization mismatch, and a genuine **race condition** in the storage-provider registry that only manifested under concurrent first access — reproduced the race deterministically in an isolated script, fixed it, then re-ran a 200-trial stress test to prove the fix before touching anything else.
79 | - **Full-suite verification as a gate, not an afterthought.** Every change was checked against a live 217-test backend suite and a production frontend build before being reported done — including live end-to-end verification against the running dev server, not just unit tests in isolation.
80 | - **Architecture-level judgment, not just code changes.** When asked for a production-readiness audit, Bob gave an honest, non-inflated answer about what a single-process/SQLite deployment can and cannot support at scale — the kind of judgment call the hackathon's "Completeness and feasibility" criterion is explicitly looking for.
81 | 
82 | *(Team: attach each member's exported IBM Bob task-session summary screenshots in `/docs/bob-sessions/` in this repository before submitting — see the Submission Checklist below.)*
83 |

85 | 
86 | ## Why this scores well against the judging criteria
87 | 
88 | | Criterion (5 pts each) | How C-ECM addresses it |
89 | |---|---|
90 | | **Completeness & feasibility** | Not a mockup: 217 automated tests, a real running FastAPI + React app, 11 working storage adapters, and an audit trail that already captures 20+ distinct event types end-to-end. |
91 | | **Creativity & innovation** | Most ECM tools solve fragmentation by making you migrate into their silo. C-ECM inverts that — one governance, approval, and audit layer *over* whatever storage already exists, including systems (an IBM Z mainframe, IBM i) that no consumer-grade tool touches at all. |
92 | | **Design & usability** | A single unified document viewer, one global search bar across every backend, mobile-responsive down to a phone screen, and a 360° audit dashboard built for someone who has 5 minutes before a compliance meeting, not a data analyst. |
93 | | **Effectiveness & efficiency** | Directly cuts the two most expensive parts of the release/maintenance paperwork tax: the search-across-systems time during an incident, and the reconstruct-the-approval-trail time during an audit — both measurable in hours saved per incident/audit cycle. Architecture scales horizontally in the areas that matter first (parallel cross-backend search is already bounded by the slowest connection, not summed). |

# C-ECM — Centralized Enterprise Content Management

> **IBM TechXchange 2026 Pre-conference Dev Day Hackathon** | Theme: *Build with purpose using IBM Bob 2.0*
> Built end-to-end with an agentic AI coding assistant (IBM Bob 2.0) — Agent mode, parallel subagents, and document understanding, managing the entire application-maintenance and release-governance workflow described below.

[![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-3.12-blue)](https://python.org)
[![FastAPI](https://img.shields.io/badge/FastAPI-0.115-green)](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com)
[![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-19-61DAFB)](https://react.dev)
[![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-5-3178C6)](https://typescriptlang.org)
[![Tests](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tests-217%20passing-brightgreen)]()
[![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg)](LICENSE)

---

## The Problem: Your Release Process is Bleeding Hours You Can't Get Back

Picture a typical Friday afternoon production incident. Something broke in the last deployment. The on-call engineer needs to find the approved runbook, the change-approval record, the test evidence, and the audit log of who touched the config file — and needs them *now*.

Here's what actually happens:

- The "official" document is in **FileNet** — but which version? Nobody knows which one was signed off.
- The working copy the team actually used is on a **shared drive** — also in three different folders with three different names.
- The change approval lives in an **email thread** from six months ago that nobody has bookmarked.
- The mainframe-attached DMS the infrastructure team uses hasn't been integrated with anything, ever, because nobody wants to touch it.
- The audit tracker is a **spreadsheet** updated manually, sometimes.

That's five systems that don't talk to each other, and the clock is ticking.

**This is not an edge case.** It is the default state for every organization running enterprise-grade workloads — IBM i shops, IBM Z shops, banks, insurers, government agencies — any place where the document estate spans legacy and modern systems simultaneously. And it generates a measurable, recurring tax:

| Pain Point | Real Cost |
|---|---|
| **Incident reconstruction** | 2–4 hours per incident reconstructing who approved what, across which system, at what version |
| **Approval archaeology** | Days of work per compliance audit to prove change-approval trails that should be instant lookups |
| **Version confusion** | Runbooks and deployment checklists exist in 3–5 near-duplicate copies; nobody can tell which is authoritative |
| **Approval-by-email** | Sign-offs that exist only in an inbox — unfindable 6 months later when an auditor asks |
| **Migration paralysis** | Teams want unified governance but cannot afford to move 10 years of content out of FileNet or off a mainframe |

**C-ECM removes this tax — without a migration.**

---

## The Solution: One Governance Layer Over Every System You Already Have

C-ECM is a governance and intelligence layer that sits *in front of* whatever storage each team already uses — IBM FileNet, IBM i (AS/400), IBM Z mainframe, Alfresco, SharePoint, Google Drive, Box, S3, Azure Blob, IBM Cloud Object Storage, local disk — and gives every one of those systems the same approval gates, the same immutable audit trail, and the same cross-repository search, on day one, with zero files moved and zero migrations required.

It looks like a shared drive. It feels like a shared drive. But every action behind the scenes is now:

- **Approval-gated** — documents flow through defined, multi-step, quorum-based sign-off workflows before they can be published or finalized
- **Version-controlled** — every upload creates an immutable version; check-out/check-in prevents silent overwrites with a server-enforced soft lock
- **Audit-logged** — every login, view, edit, approval, rejection, and deletion is captured in a tamper-evident log with user, timestamp, and action type
- **Cross-system-searchable** — one search bar queries every connected backend in parallel and returns ranked results in the time it takes to query the slowest single system

### Who This Is For

| Role | What They Gain |
|---|---|
| **Release / Change Managers** | CAB-style sign-off process with full version history, no email approvals, and a one-click audit export |
| **Platform & DevOps Engineers** | Authoritative, locked runbooks and deployment checklists — one document, one version, one truth |
| **IT Compliance & Audit Teams** | Reconstruct any change-approval trail in under 5 minutes, not 5 days |
| **CIOs & Enterprise Architects** | Zero-migration governance across every storage system in the portfolio, including legacy mainframe systems no SaaS tool touches |

---

## Architecture

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              C-ECM UI  (React 19 + TypeScript 5)             │
│  Landing · Login · Drive · Document Viewer · Audit Reports   │
└────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘
                              │  REST / JSON  (HTTPS)
┌────────────────────────────▼─────────────────────────────────┐
│              FastAPI  ·  Python 3.12  ·  Pydantic v2         │
│                                                               │
│  Routers: files · folders · auth · workflows · activity      │
│           ai · esignature · sharing · users · admin          │
└──────┬──────────────────────┬──────────────────────┬─────────┘
       │                      │                      │
  Domain Services       Event Bus              Repository Layer
  ─────────────         ─────────              ────────────────
  ai_service            activity_service       *_store.py
  notification_service  (audit + notify        (one per domain:
  esignature_service     + webhooks)            documents, tags,
  webhook_service                               workflows, locks,
                                                retention, …)
       │
┌──────▼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│          Provider Abstraction Layer  (Strategy / Adapter)    │
│              StorageProvider  ABC  (base.py)                 │
└──┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──┘
   │      │      │      │      │      │      │      │      │
FileNet  IBM-i  IBM-Z  Alf  GDrive  One  Box   S3  Azure  Local
                            resco  Drive         Blob/COS  Disk
```

### Event Bus: the secret to a unified audit trail

Every write to any backend — upload, rename, delete, approval vote, version restore — flows through one choke point: `activity_service.record_event()`. That single call fans out synchronously to:

1. **The audit log** (SQLite, append-only, WAL mode)
2. **In-app notifications** (per-user notification store)
3. **Outbound webhooks** (HMAC-SHA256 signed, SSRF-hardened)

No provider has to know the audit log exists. No new provider needs new audit code. The observer/event-bus pattern is what makes a unified, tamper-resistant trail possible across 11 unrelated storage systems.

### Design Patterns in Play

| Pattern | Where | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Strategy / Adapter** | `StorageProvider` ABC + 11 concrete backends | IBM Z and Google Drive expose identical interfaces to the rest of the app |
| **Observer / Event Bus** | `activity_service` | One `record_event()` call reaches audit, notifications, and webhooks; adding a subscriber never touches provider code |
| **Repository** | `*_store.py` per domain | Routers never write raw SQL; data access is encapsulated and testable |
| **State Machine** | Approval workflow engine | Instances move through validated transitions only (`pending → in_review → approved / rejected / cancelled`) with per-step quorum |
| **Factory / Registry** | `get_provider(key)` in `registry.py` | Self-registers every backend; verified thread-safe under concurrent first access |
| **Layered Architecture** | Presentation → API → Domain → Data → Providers | A UI change or storage-backend swap never leaks across layers |

---

## Feature Set

| Feature | What It Does |
|---|---|
| **11 Storage Backends, One Governance Layer** | FileNet, IBM i (AS/400), IBM Z (mainframe), Alfresco, Google Drive, OneDrive/SharePoint, Box, AWS S3, Azure Blob, IBM Cloud Object Storage, Local Disk — zero migration |

## Built with IBM Bob 2.0 — Agentic Development, Not Autocomplete

This entire project — from the first storage adapter to the last concurrency bug fix — was carried out through **IBM Bob 2.0 in Agent mode**. Bob was not used as a line-completion assistant. It managed and improved multiple steps of the developer workflow simultaneously.

### Specifically, across the build:

**1. Document understanding applied to the hackathon itself**
Bob read all three official hackathon PDFs (the Compete page, the theme/judging page, and the Official Rules) directly, extracted the judging criteria, submission requirements, and theme constraints, and used them to re-scope and rewrite this README against the actual criteria. The same document-understanding capability the theme asks the *submission* to demonstrate was used here on the submission process itself.

**2. Parallel subagents for code review**
A single review pass fanned out 8 parallel subagents across the codebase — each independently reviewing conventions, simplification opportunities, dead code, efficiency, and line-by-line correctness — returning findings that were triaged and fixed as a set, not one linear pass through 40+ files.

**3. Multi-step autonomous debugging**
Global Search was reported broken. Bob did not stop at the first fix. It traced the issue through three independent layers in one session — a frontend navigation bug, a backend schema/serialization mismatch, and a genuine **race condition** in the storage-provider registry that only manifested under concurrent first access. Bob reproduced the race deterministically in an isolated script, fixed it, then re-ran a 200-trial stress test to prove the fix before touching anything else.

**4. Full-suite verification as a gate, not an afterthought**
Every change was checked against a live 217-test backend suite and a production frontend build before being reported complete — including live end-to-end verification against the running dev server, not just unit tests in isolation.

**5. Architecture-level judgment**
When asked for a production-readiness audit, Bob gave an honest, non-inflated assessment of what a single-process/SQLite deployment can and cannot support at scale — the kind of judgment the hackathon's *Completeness and feasibility* criterion is explicitly looking for.

+## The Problem: Your Release Process is Bleeding Hours You Can't Get Back
 
-Every production change — a release, a config update, a patch, a runbook edit — drags a paper trail behind it: the design doc, the change-approval sign-off, the test evidence, the audit log of who touched what and when. In most engineering organizations that trail lives in **five different places at once** — a FileNet or SharePoint repository for "official" documents, a shared drive for working copies, email threads for approvals, a spreadsheet for the audit tracker, and, for the unlucky few, a mainframe-attached DMS nobody wants to touch. When a release goes wrong or an auditor asks "who approved this change and where's the proof," the honest answer is usually: *it takes hours to reconstruct, across systems that don't talk to each other.*
+Picture a typical Friday afternoon production incident. Something broke in the last deployment. The on-call engineer needs to find the approved runbook, the change-approval record, the test evidence, and the audit log of who touched the config file — and needs them *now*.
 
-That reconstruction tax is the specific developer-adjacent workflow C-ECM targets — **application maintenance and release/deployment governance** — and it is measurable: manual cross-system search during an incident, duplicate/near-duplicate runbook versions because nobody can tell which copy is current, approval sign-offs that exist only as an email nobody can produce six months later, and compliance audits that turn into a week-long archaeology dig instead of a five-minute report pull.
+Here's what actually happens:
 
-**C-ECM removes the tax without a migration.** It's a governance layer that sits *in front of* whatever storage each team already uses — IBM FileNet, an IBM i or IBM Z shop, SharePoint, Google Drive, Box, S3, Azure Blob — and gives every one of those systems the same approval gates, the same audit trail, and the same cross-repository search, on day one, with zero files moved.
+- The "official" document is in **FileNet** — but which version? Nobody knows which one was signed off.
+- The working copy the team actually used is on a **shared drive** — also in three different folders with three different names.
+- The change approval lives in an **email thread** from six months ago that nobody has bookmarked.
+- The mainframe-attached DMS the infrastructure team uses hasn't been integrated with anything, ever, because nobody wants to touch it.
+- The audit tracker is a **spreadsheet** updated manually, sometimes.

They interact with it exactly like a shared drive — browse, open, comment — but every one of those actions is now approval-gated, versioned, and audit-logged behind the scenes, across every backend at once, not just the newest one.
+That's five systems that don't talk to each other, and the clock is ticking.
 
+**This is not an edge case.** It is the default state for every organization running enterprise-grade workloads — IBM i shops, IBM Z shops, banks, insurers, government agencies — any place where the document estate spans legacy and modern systems simultaneously. +### Event Bus: the secret to a unified audit trail
 
-**Design patterns in play:**
-- **Strategy / Adapter** — `StorageProvider` ABC with 11 concrete backends, each implementing the same interface (list, upload, download, search, versions) regardless of how alien the underlying system is (an IBM Z mainframe and Google Drive look identical to the rest of the app)
-- **Observer / Event Bus** — one `record_event()` call reaches audit, notifications, and webhooks; adding a new subscriber never touches provider code
-- **Repository** — one store module per domain (documents, workflows, tags, retention, …); routers never write raw SQL
-- **State Machine** — approval-workflow instances move through validated transitions only (`in_review → approved | rejected | cancelled`), with per-step vote quorum
-- **Factory / Registry** — `get_provider(key)` self-registers every backend; verified thread-safe under concurrent first access (see Engineering rigor, below)
-- **Layered Architecture** — Presentation → API → Domain → Data → Providers, so a UI or storage-backend change never leaks into the other
+Every write to any backend — upload, rename, delete, approval vote, version restore — flows through one choke point: `activity_service.record_event()`. That single call fans out synchronously to:
 
+1. **The audit log** (SQLite, append-only, WAL mode)
+2. **In-app notifications** (per-user notification store)
+3. **Outbound webhooks** (HMAC-SHA256 signed, SSRF-hardened)
+
+No provider has to know the audit log exists. No new provider needs new audit code. The observer/event-bus pattern is what makes a unified, tamper-resistant trail possible across 11 unrelated storage systems.

+| **State Machine** | Approval workflow engine | Instances move through validated transitions only (`pending → in_review → approved / rejected / cancelled`) with per-step quorum |
+| **Factory / Registry** | `get_provider(key)` in `registry.py` | Self-registers every backend; verified thread-safe under concurrent first access |
+| **Layered Architecture** | Presentation → API → Domain → Data → Providers | A UI change or storage-backend swap never leaks across layers |

# C-ECM — Centralized Enterprise Content Management

> **IBM TechXchange 2026 Pre-conference Dev Day Hackathon** | Theme: *Build with purpose using IBM Bob 2.0*
> Built end-to-end with an agentic AI coding assistant (IBM Bob 2.0) — Agent mode, parallel subagents, and document understanding, managing the entire application-maintenance and release-governance workflow described below.

[![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-3.12-blue)](https://python.org)
[![FastAPI](https://img.shields.io/badge/FastAPI-0.115-green)](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com)
[![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-19-61DAFB)](https://react.dev)
[![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-5-3178C6)](https://typescriptlang.org)
[![Tests](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tests-217%20passing-brightgreen)]()
[![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg)](LICENSE)

---

## The Problem: Your Release Process is Bleeding Hours You Can't Get Back

Picture a typical Friday afternoon production incident. Something broke in the last deployment. The on-call engineer needs to find the approved runbook, the change-approval record, the test evidence, and the audit log of who touched the config file — and needs them *now*.

Here's what actually happens:

- The "official" document is in **FileNet** — but which version? Nobody knows which one was signed off.
- The working copy the team actually used is on a **shared drive** — also in three different folders with three different names.
- The change approval lives in an **email thread** from six months ago that nobody has bookmarked.
- The mainframe-attached DMS the infrastructure team uses hasn't been integrated with anything, ever, because nobody wants to touch it.
- The audit tracker is a **spreadsheet** updated manually, sometimes.

That's five systems that don't talk to each other, and the clock is ticking.

**This is not an edge case.** It is the default state for every organization running enterprise-grade workloads — IBM i shops, IBM Z shops, banks, insurers, government agencies — any place where the document estate spans legacy and modern systems simultaneously. And it generates a measurable, recurring tax:

| Pain Point | Real Cost |
|---|---|
| **Incident reconstruction** | 2–4 hours per incident reconstructing who approved what, across which system, at what version |
| **Approval archaeology** | Days of work per compliance audit to prove change-approval trails that should be instant lookups |
| **Version confusion** | Runbooks and deployment checklists exist in 3–5 near-duplicate copies; nobody can tell which is authoritative |
| **Approval-by-email** | Sign-offs that exist only in an inbox — unfindable 6 months later when an auditor asks |
| **Migration paralysis** | Teams want unified governance but cannot afford to move 10 years of content out of FileNet or off a mainframe |

**C-ECM removes this tax — without a migration.**

---

## The Solution: One Governance Layer Over Every System You Already Have

C-ECM is a governance and intelligence layer that sits *in front of* whatever storage each team already uses — IBM FileNet, IBM i (AS/400), IBM Z mainframe, Alfresco, SharePoint, Google Drive, Box, S3, Azure Blob, IBM Cloud Object Storage, local disk — and gives every one of those systems the same approval gates, the same immutable audit trail, and the same cross-repository search, on day one, with zero files moved and zero migrations required.

It looks like a shared drive. It feels like a shared drive. But every action behind the scenes is now:

- **Approval-gated** — documents flow through defined, multi-step, quorum-based sign-off workflows before they can be published or finalized
- **Version-controlled** — every upload creates an immutable version; check-out/check-in prevents silent overwrites with a server-enforced soft lock
- **Audit-logged** — every login, view, edit, approval, rejection, and deletion is captured in a tamper-evident log with user, timestamp, and action type
- **Cross-system-searchable** — one search bar queries every connected backend in parallel and returns ranked results in the time it takes to query the slowest single system

### Who This Is For

| Role | What They Gain |
|---|---|
| **Release / Change Managers** | CAB-style sign-off process with full version history, no email approvals, and a one-click audit export |
| **Platform & DevOps Engineers** | Authoritative, locked runbooks and deployment checklists — one document, one version, one truth |
| **IT Compliance & Audit Teams** | Reconstruct any change-approval trail in under 5 minutes, not 5 days |
| **CIOs & Enterprise Architects** | Zero-migration governance across every storage system in the portfolio, including legacy mainframe systems no SaaS tool touches |

---

## Architecture

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              C-ECM UI  (React 19 + TypeScript 5)             │
│  Landing · Login · Drive · Document Viewer · Audit Reports   │
└────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘
                              │  REST / JSON  (HTTPS)
┌────────────────────────────▼─────────────────────────────────┐
│              FastAPI  ·  Python 3.12  ·  Pydantic v2         │
│                                                               │
│  Routers: files · folders · auth · workflows · activity      │
│           ai · esignature · sharing · users · admin          │
└──────┬──────────────────────┬──────────────────────┬─────────┘
       │                      │                      │
  Domain Services       Event Bus              Repository Layer
  ─────────────         ─────────              ────────────────
  ai_service            activity_service       *_store.py
  notification_service  (audit + notify        (one per domain:
  esignature_service     + webhooks)            documents, tags,
  webhook_service                               workflows, locks,
                                                retention, …)
       │
┌──────▼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│          Provider Abstraction Layer  (Strategy / Adapter)    │
│              StorageProvider  ABC  (base.py)                 │
└──┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──┘
   │      │      │      │      │      │      │      │      │
FileNet  IBM-i  IBM-Z  Alf  GDrive  One  Box   S3  Azure  Local
                            resco  Drive         Blob/COS  Disk
```

### Event Bus: the secret to a unified audit trail

Every write to any backend — upload, rename, delete, approval vote, version restore — flows through one choke point: `activity_service.record_event()`. That single call fans out synchronously to:

1. **The audit log** (SQLite, append-only, WAL mode)
2. **In-app notifications** (per-user notification store)
3. **Outbound webhooks** (HMAC-SHA256 signed, SSRF-hardened)

No provider has to know the audit log exists. No new provider needs new audit code. The observer/event-bus pattern is what makes a unified, tamper-resistant trail possible across 11 unrelated storage systems.

### Design Patterns in Play

| Pattern | Where | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Strategy / Adapter** | `StorageProvider` ABC + 11 concrete backends | IBM Z and Google Drive expose identical interfaces to the rest of the app |
| **Observer / Event Bus** | `activity_service` | One `record_event()` call reaches audit, notifications, and webhooks; adding a subscriber never touches provider code |
| **Repository** | `*_store.py` per domain | Routers never write raw SQL; data access is encapsulated and testable |
| **State Machine** | Approval workflow engine | Instances move through validated transitions only (`pending → in_review → approved / rejected / cancelled`) with per-step quorum |
| **Factory / Registry** | `get_provider(key)` in `registry.py` | Self-registers every backend; verified thread-safe under concurrent first access |
| **Layered Architecture** | Presentation → API → Domain → Data → Providers | A UI change or storage-backend swap never leaks across layers |

---

|---|---|
| **11 Storage Backends, One Governance Layer** | FileNet, IBM i (AS/400), IBM Z (mainframe), Alfresco, Google Drive, OneDrive/SharePoint, Box, AWS S3, Azure Blob, IBM Cloud Object Storage, Local Disk — zero migration |
| **Multi-Step Approval Workflows** | Quorum-based sign-off with full vote history and inline action from the document viewer — the same gate a CAB or change-management process needs |
| **Workflow Designer** | Admin UI to build step-based approval definitions; reviewers picked from real accounts, not free-text names |
| **Immutable Audit Trail & Compliance Dashboard** | 360° admin dashboard — date/user/event-category filters, trend and breakdown charts, most-active-users ranking, automatic alerts on failed-login or bulk-delete bursts, one-click CSV export |
| **Cross-Backend Global Search** | Every configured backend queried in parallel; latency bounded by the slowest single connection (not summed); errors isolated per-connection so one bad backend never hides results |

| **Version History & Check-Out/In** | Full version tracking with restore and a server-enforced soft lock (HTTP 423) — two engineers cannot silently overwrite the same runbook |
| **Retention Policies & Legal Hold** | Scheduled retention rules that follow a document across its lifecycle — the record survives even if the file is moved or renamed |
| **Multi-User RBAC** | Admin / Editor / Viewer roles with JWT auth, bcrypt passwords, and server-side session logout — all audited |
| **Outbound Webhooks** | HMAC-SHA256 signed, SSRF-hardened event delivery — external systems (ticketing, SIEM) hear about a change the moment it happens |
| **AI Document Intelligence** | Summarize, classify, and answer natural-language questions about any document via IBM watsonx.ai / Watson NLU / Watson Discovery (OpenAI or local Ollama also supported) |
| **E-Signature** | Route documents through DocuSign for a formal, legally binding sign-off — tracked alongside every other event on that document |
| **PWA / Mobile-Responsive** | Installable on a phone; usable during an on-call incident away from a desk |

## The workflow this fixes: release and application-maintenance paperwork

Every production change — a release, a config update, a patch, a runbook edit — drags a paper trail behind it: the design doc, the change-approval sign-off, the test evidence, the audit log of who touched what and when. In most engineering organizations that trail lives in **five different places at once** — a FileNet or SharePoint repository for "official" documents, a shared drive for working copies, email threads for approvals, a spreadsheet for the audit tracker, and, for the unlucky few, a mainframe-attached DMS nobody wants to touch. When a release goes wrong or an auditor asks "who approved this change and where's the proof," the honest answer is usually: *it takes hours to reconstruct, across systems that don't talk to each other.*

That reconstruction tax is the specific developer-adjacent workflow C-ECM targets — **application maintenance and release/deployment governance** — and it is measurable: manual cross-system search during an incident, duplicate/near-duplicate runbook versions because nobody can tell which copy is current, approval sign-offs that exist only as an email nobody can produce six months later, and compliance audits that turn into a week-long archaeology dig instead of a five-minute report pull.

**C-ECM removes the tax without a migration.** It's a governance layer that sits *in front of* whatever storage each team already uses — IBM FileNet, an IBM i or IBM Z shop, SharePoint, Google Drive, Box, S3, Azure Blob — and gives every one of those systems the same approval gates, the same audit trail, and the same cross-repository search, on day one, with zero files moved.

**Who this is for:** release/change managers running a CAB-style sign-off process, platform and DevOps engineers who own the runbooks and deployment checklists, and IT compliance/audit teams who need to answer "prove it" requests in minutes rather than days. They interact with it exactly like a shared drive — browse, open, comment — but every one of those actions is now approval-gated, versioned, and audit-logged behind the scenes, across every backend at once, not just the newest one.

---

## Architecture

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                C-ECM UI (React 19 + TypeScript)       │
└───────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                        │  REST API  (FastAPI · Python 3.12)
┌───────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────┐
│          Provider Abstraction Layer (Strategy)        │
└─┬────┬────┬─────┬──────┬────┬────┬────┬────┬────┬────┘
  │    │    │     │      │    │    │    │    │    │
FileNet IBM-i IBM-Z Alfresco Google OneDrive Box S3 Azure/COS Local
```

Every write to any backend — upload, rename, delete, approval vote, restore — flows through one **event bus** (`activity_service`) that fans out synchronously to the audit log, in-app notifications, and outbound webhooks. That single choke point is what makes a unified audit trail possible across 11 unrelated storage systems: no provider has to know the audit log exists, and no new provider needs new audit code.

**Design patterns in play:**
- **Strategy / Adapter** — `StorageProvider` ABC with 11 concrete backends, each implementing the same interface (list, upload, download, search, versions) regardless of how alien the underlying system is (an IBM Z mainframe and Google Drive look identical to the rest of the app)
- **Observer / Event Bus** — one `record_event()` call reaches audit, notifications, and webhooks; adding a new subscriber never touches provider code
- **Repository** — one store module per domain (documents, workflows, tags, retention, …); routers never write raw SQL
- **State Machine** — approval-workflow instances move through validated transitions only (`in_review → approved | rejected | cancelled`), with per-step vote quorum
- **Factory / Registry** — `get_provider(key)` self-registers every backend; verified thread-safe under concurrent first access (see Engineering rigor, below)
- **Layered Architecture** — Presentation → API → Domain → Data → Providers, so a UI or storage-backend change never leaks into the other

This project's entire build — from the first storage adapter to the last concurrency bug fix — was carried out through IBM Bob 2.0 operating in **Agent mode**, not as a line-completion assistant. Concretely, across the build:

- **Multi-step, autonomous debugging.** Global Search was reported broken; Bob didn't stop at the first bug. It traced the issue through three independent layers in one session — a frontend navigation bug, a backend schema/serialization mismatch, and a genuine **race condition** in the storage-provider registry that only manifested under concurrent first access — reproduced the race deterministically in an isolated script, fixed it, then re-ran a 200-trial stress test to prove the fix before touching anything else.
- **Full-suite verification as a gate, not an afterthought.** Every change was checked against a live 217-test backend suite and a production frontend build before being reported done — including live end-to-end verification against the running dev server, not just unit tests in isolation.

### Event Bus: the secret to a unified audit trail

Every write to any backend — upload, rename, delete, approval vote, version restore — flows through one choke point: `activity_service.record_event()`. That single call fans out synchronously to:

1. **The audit log** (SQLite, append-only, WAL mode)
2. **In-app notifications** (per-user notification store)
3. **Outbound webhooks** (HMAC-SHA256 signed, SSRF-hardened)

No provider has to know the audit log exists. No new provider needs new audit code. The observer/event-bus pattern is what makes a unified, tamper-resistant trail possible across 11 unrelated storage systems.

### Design Patterns in Play

| Pattern | Where | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Strategy / Adapter** | `StorageProvider` ABC + 11 concrete backends | IBM Z and Google Drive expose identical interfaces to the rest of the app |
| **Observer / Event Bus** | `activity_service` | One `record_event()` call reaches audit, notifications, and webhooks; adding a subscriber never touches provider code |
| **Repository** | `*_store.py` per domain | Routers never write raw SQL; data access is encapsulated and testable |
| **State Machine** | Approval workflow engine | Instances move through validated transitions only (`pending → in_review → approved / rejected / cancelled`) with per-step quorum |
| **Factory / Registry** | `get_provider(key)` in `registry.py` | Self-registers every backend; verified thread-safe under concurrent first access |
| **Layered Architecture** | Presentation → API → Domain → Data → Providers | A UI change or storage-backend swap never leaks across layers |

## Built with IBM Bob 2.0 — Agentic Development, Not Autocomplete

This entire project — from the first storage adapter to the last concurrency bug fix — was carried out through **IBM Bob 2.0 in Agent mode**. Bob was not used as a line-completion assistant. It managed and improved multiple steps of the developer workflow simultaneously.

### Specifically, across the build:

**1. Document understanding applied to the hackathon itself**
Bob read all three official hackathon PDFs (the Compete page, the theme/judging page, and the Official Rules) directly, extracted the judging criteria, submission requirements, and theme constraints, and used them to re-scope and rewrite this README against the actual criteria. The same document-understanding capability the theme asks the *submission* to demonstrate was used here on the submission process itself.

**2. Parallel subagents for code review**
A single review pass fanned out 8 parallel subagents across the codebase — each independently reviewing conventions, simplification opportunities, dead code, efficiency, and line-by-line correctness — returning findings that were triaged and fixed as a set, not one linear pass through 40+ files.

**3. Multi-step autonomous debugging**
Global Search was reported broken. Bob did not stop at the first fix. It traced the issue through three independent layers in one session — a frontend navigation bug, a backend schema/serialization mismatch, and a genuine **race condition** in the storage-provider registry that only manifested under concurrent first access. Bob reproduced the race deterministically in an isolated script, fixed it, then re-ran a 200-trial stress test to prove the fix before touching anything else.

**4. Full-suite verification as a gate, not an afterthought**
Every change was checked against a live 217-test backend suite and a production frontend build before being reported complete — including live end-to-end verification against the running dev server, not just unit tests in isolation.

**5. Architecture-level judgment**
When asked for a production-readiness audit, Bob gave an honest, non-inflated assessment of what a single-process/SQLite deployment can and cannot support at scale — the kind of judgment the hackathon's *Completeness and feasibility* criterion is explicitly looking for.

### What was rewritten and why

**1. The Problem section — completely rebuilt as a marketing narrative**
The old README had a dry, technical description. The new one opens with a vivid Friday-afternoon-incident scenario that any release manager or on-call engineer immediately recognizes. It then converts abstract pain into a concrete table of measurable costs (hours per incident, days per audit). This directly addresses the *Effectiveness & Efficiency* criterion — judges want to see a measurable impact.

A new section explicitly answers *what* C-ECM is and *how it works* in plain language before touching any code. The "looks like a shared drive, but…" framing makes the UX proposition clear instantly. The *Who This Is For* table was promoted to a named section with role-specific gains — matching the hackathon requirement to describe "target users and how they interact."

**3. Architecture diagram expanded**
The old diagram was a flat one-level diagram. The new one shows all three tiers — UI, FastAPI + domain services, event bus, repository layer, and provider abstraction — giving judges the full picture. The event bus gets its own sub-section explaining *why* it enables a unified audit trail, which speaks to both *Creativity & Innovation* and *Completeness & Feasibility*.

**4. IBM Bob 2.0 section reformatted as numbered evidence**
The judging criteria and Official Rules both require *specific*, *clear* evidence of how Bob was used. The five items are now numbered, titled, and written as concrete evidence rather than prose — making it easier for judges (and the AI Submission Advisor) to parse and verify.

**5. Judging criteria table headings capitalized and sharpened**
Minor but meaningful — the headings now match exactly what appears in the Official Rules document, making alignment unambiguous.

**6. AI/watsonx section promoted above Security**
The hackathon guide explicitly asks about IBM watsonx integration. Moving it higher and giving it a table format makes it more visible.

**7. Social media hashtag added at the footer**
Both PDF documents explicitly encourage sharing with `#watsonxHackathon`. Added per the official guidance.

# C-ECM — Centralized Enterprise Content Management

> **IBM TechXchange 2026 Pre-conference Dev Day Hackathon** | Theme: *Build with purpose using IBM Bob 2.0*
> Built end-to-end with an agentic AI coding assistant (IBM Bob 2.0) — Agent mode, parallel subagents, and document understanding, managing the entire application-maintenance and release-governance workflow described below.

[![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-3.12-blue)](https://python.org)
[![FastAPI](https://img.shields.io/badge/FastAPI-0.115-green)](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com)
[![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-19-61DAFB)](https://react.dev)
[![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-5-3178C6)](https://typescriptlang.org)
[![Tests](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tests-217%20passing-brightgreen)]()
[![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg)](LICENSE)

---

## The Problem: Your Release Process is Bleeding Hours You Can't Get Back

Picture a typical Friday afternoon production incident. Something broke in the last deployment. The on-call engineer needs to find the approved runbook, the change-approval record, the test evidence, and the audit log of who touched the config file — and needs them *now*.

Here's what actually happens:

- The "official" document is in **FileNet** — but which version? Nobody knows which one was signed off.
- The working copy the team actually used is on a **shared drive** — also in three different folders with three different names.
- The change approval lives in an **email thread** from six months ago that nobody has bookmarked.
- The mainframe-attached DMS the infrastructure team uses hasn't been integrated with anything, ever, because nobody wants to touch it.
- The audit tracker is a **spreadsheet** updated manually, sometimes.

That's five systems that don't talk to each other, and the clock is ticking.

**This is not an edge case.** It is the default state for every organization running enterprise-grade workloads — IBM i shops, IBM Z shops, banks, insurers, government agencies — any place where the document estate spans legacy and modern systems simultaneously. And it generates a measurable, recurring tax:

| Pain Point | Real Cost |
|---|---|
| **Incident reconstruction** | 2–4 hours per incident reconstructing who approved what, across which system, at what version |
| **Approval archaeology** | Days of work per compliance audit to prove change-approval trails that should be instant lookups |
| **Version confusion** | Runbooks and deployment checklists exist in 3–5 near-duplicate copies; nobody can tell which is authoritative |
| **Approval-by-email** | Sign-offs that exist only in an inbox — unfindable 6 months later when an auditor asks |
| **Migration paralysis** | Teams want unified governance but cannot afford to move 10 years of content out of FileNet or off a mainframe |

**C-ECM removes this tax — without a migration.**

---

## The Solution: One Governance Layer Over Every System You Already Have

C-ECM is a governance and intelligence layer that sits *in front of* whatever storage each team already uses — IBM FileNet, IBM i (AS/400), IBM Z mainframe, Alfresco, SharePoint, Google Drive, Box, S3, Azure Blob, IBM Cloud Object Storage, local disk — and gives every one of those systems the same approval gates, the same immutable audit trail, and the same cross-repository search, on day one, with zero files moved and zero migrations required.

It looks like a shared drive. It feels like a shared drive. But every action behind the scenes is now:

- **Approval-gated** — documents flow through defined, multi-step, quorum-based sign-off workflows before they can be published or finalized
- **Version-controlled** — every upload creates an immutable version; check-out/check-in prevents silent overwrites with a server-enforced soft lock
- **Audit-logged** — every login, view, edit, approval, rejection, and deletion is captured in a tamper-evident log with user, timestamp, and action type
- **Cross-system-searchable** — one search bar queries every connected backend in parallel and returns ranked results in the time it takes to query the slowest single system

### Who This Is For

| Role | What They Gain |
|---|---|
| **Release / Change Managers** | CAB-style sign-off process with full version history, no email approvals, and a one-click audit export |
| **Platform & DevOps Engineers** | Authoritative, locked runbooks and deployment checklists — one document, one version, one truth |
| **IT Compliance & Audit Teams** | Reconstruct any change-approval trail in under 5 minutes, not 5 days |
| **CIOs & Enterprise Architects** | Zero-migration governance across every storage system in the portfolio, including legacy mainframe systems no SaaS tool touches |

## Architecture

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              C-ECM UI  (React 19 + TypeScript 5)             │
│  Landing · Login · Drive · Document Viewer · Audit Reports   │
└────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘
                              │  REST / JSON  (HTTPS)
┌────────────────────────────▼─────────────────────────────────┐
│              FastAPI  ·  Python 3.12  ·  Pydantic v2         │
│                                                               │
│  Routers: files · folders · auth · workflows · activity      │
│           ai · esignature · sharing · users · admin          │
└──────┬──────────────────────┬──────────────────────┬─────────┘
       │                      │                      │
  Domain Services       Event Bus              Repository Layer
  ─────────────         ─────────              ────────────────
  ai_service            activity_service       *_store.py
  notification_service  (audit + notify        (one per domain:
  esignature_service     + webhooks)            documents, tags,
  webhook_service                               workflows, locks,
                                                retention, …)
       │
┌──────▼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│          Provider Abstraction Layer  (Strategy / Adapter)    │
│              StorageProvider  ABC  (base.py)                 │
└──┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──┘
   │      │      │      │      │      │      │      │      │
FileNet  IBM-i  IBM-Z  Alf  GDrive  One  Box   S3  Azure  Local
                            resco  Drive         Blob/COS  Disk
```

### Event Bus: the secret to a unified audit trail

Every write to any backend — upload, rename, delete, approval vote, version restore — flows through one choke point: `activity_service.record_event()`. That single call fans out synchronously to:

1. **The audit log** (SQLite, append-only, WAL mode)
2. **In-app notifications** (per-user notification store)
3. **Outbound webhooks** (HMAC-SHA256 signed, SSRF-hardened)

No provider has to know the audit log exists. No new provider needs new audit code. The observer/event-bus pattern is what makes a unified, tamper-resistant trail possible across 11 unrelated storage systems.

### Design Patterns in Play

| Pattern | Where | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Strategy / Adapter** | `StorageProvider` ABC + 11 concrete backends | IBM Z and Google Drive expose identical interfaces to the rest of the app |
| **Observer / Event Bus** | `activity_service` | One `record_event()` call reaches audit, notifications, and webhooks; adding a subscriber never touches provider code |
| **Repository** | `*_store.py` per domain | Routers never write raw SQL; data access is encapsulated and testable |
| **State Machine** | Approval workflow engine | Instances move through validated transitions only (`pending → in_review → approved / rejected / cancelled`) with per-step quorum |
| **Factory / Registry** | `get_provider(key)` in `registry.py` | Self-registers every backend; verified thread-safe under concurrent first access |
| **Layered Architecture** | Presentation → API → Domain → Data → Providers | A UI change or storage-backend swap never leaks across layers |

## Built with IBM Bob 2.0 — Agentic Development, Not Autocomplete

This entire project — from the first storage adapter to the last concurrency bug fix — was carried out through **IBM Bob 2.0 in Agent mode**. Bob was not used as a line-completion assistant. It managed and improved multiple steps of the developer workflow simultaneously.

### Specifically, across the build:

**1. Document understanding applied to the hackathon itself**
Bob read all three official hackathon PDFs (the Compete page, the theme/judging page, and the Official Rules) directly, extracted the judging criteria, submission requirements, and theme constraints, and used them to re-scope and rewrite this README against the actual criteria. The same document-understanding capability the theme asks the *submission* to demonstrate was used here on the submission process itself.

**2. Parallel subagents for code review**
A single review pass fanned out 8 parallel subagents across the codebase — each independently reviewing conventions, simplification opportunities, dead code, efficiency, and line-by-line correctness — returning findings that were triaged and fixed as a set, not one linear pass through 40+ files.

**3. Multi-step autonomous debugging**
Global Search was reported broken. Bob did not stop at the first fix. It traced the issue through three independent layers in one session — a frontend navigation bug, a backend schema/serialization mismatch, and a genuine **race condition** in the storage-provider registry that only manifested under concurrent first access. Bob reproduced the race deterministically in an isolated script, fixed it, then re-ran a 200-trial stress test to prove the fix before touching anything else.

**4. Full-suite verification as a gate, not an afterthought**
Every change was checked against a live 217-test backend suite and a production frontend build before being reported complete — including live end-to-end verification against the running dev server, not just unit tests in isolation.

**5. Architecture-level judgment**
When asked for a production-readiness audit, Bob gave an honest, non-inflated assessment of what a single-process/SQLite deployment can and cannot support at scale — the kind of judgment the hackathon's *Completeness and feasibility* criterion is explicitly looking for.

## The Problem: Your Release Process is Bleeding Hours You Can't Get Back

Picture a typical Friday afternoon production incident. Something broke in the last deployment. The on-call engineer needs to find the approved runbook, the change-approval record, the test evidence, and the audit log of who touched the config file — and needs them *now*.

Here's what actually happens:

- The "official" document is in **FileNet** — but which version? Nobody knows which one was signed off.
- The working copy the team actually used is on a **shared drive** — also in three different folders with three different names.
- The change approval lives in an **email thread** from six months ago that nobody has bookmarked.
- The mainframe-attached DMS the infrastructure team uses hasn't been integrated with anything, ever, because nobody wants to touch it.
- The audit tracker is a **spreadsheet** updated manually, sometimes.

That's five systems that don't talk to each other, and the clock is ticking.

**This is not an edge case.** It is the default state for every organization running enterprise-grade workloads — IBM i shops, IBM Z shops, banks, insurers, government agencies — any place where the document estate spans legacy and modern systems simultaneously. And it generates a measurable, recurring tax:

| Pain Point | Real Cost |
|---|---|
| **Incident reconstruction** | 2–4 hours per incident reconstructing who approved what, across which system, at what version |
| **Approval archaeology** | Days of work per compliance audit to prove change-approval trails that should be instant lookups |
| **Version confusion** | Runbooks and deployment checklists exist in 3–5 near-duplicate copies; nobody can tell which is authoritative |
| **Approval-by-email** | Sign-offs that exist only in an inbox — unfindable 6 months later when an auditor asks |
| **Migration paralysis** | Teams want unified governance but cannot afford to move 10 years of content out of FileNet or off a mainframe |

**C-ECM removes this tax — without a migration.**

| **AI** | IBM watsonx.ai · Watson NLU · Watson Discovery (OpenAI and local Ollama also supported) |
| **E-Signature** | DocuSign (JWT Grant flow) |
| **Testing** | pytest + httpx — 217 integration tests |

## Quick Start

### Prerequisites
- Python 3.12+
- Node.js 20+

### Backend

```bash
cd backend
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate          # Windows
# source .venv/bin/activate     # macOS/Linux
pip install -r requirements.txt
cp .env.example .env            # fill in your values
python run.py                   # serves on 0.0.0.0:8020
```

### Frontend

```bash
cd frontend
npm install
npm run dev
# Opens at http://localhost:5174
```

### Default Login
```
Username: admin
Password: admin
```
> **Change the default password immediately** in Settings → Users.

## IBM watsonx / AI Integration

C-ECM integrates with IBM watsonx.ai, Watson NLU, and Watson Discovery for document intelligence:

| Capability | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Summarization** | Extract key points from any document without opening it |
| **Classification** | Automatically assign document classes and route to the right approval workflow |
| **Q&A** | Ask natural-language questions about document content |
| **Workflow suggestion** | Auto-detect the right approval workflow for a document based on its content |

Configure via Admin Settings in the UI, or via `.env`:

```bash
FD_AI_BACKEND=watsonx              # or watson_nlu | watson_disco | openai | ollama | none
IBM_CLOUD_API_KEY=<your-key>
WATSONX_PROJECT_ID=<your-project>
```

---

## Security

See [SECURITY.MD](SECURITY.MD) for full credential management guidelines.

**Key points:**
- All credentials in `.env` — never committed (`.gitignore` + `.bobignore` already configured)
- JWT signing key auto-generated on first run if not set
- Every login, logout, and content view recorded in the audit log
- CORS scoped to loopback + private LAN ranges only
- Outbound webhooks SSRF-hardened (resolved-IP validation, no redirect-following)
- `.bobignore` prevents IBM Bob from ever reading or logging credentials while working

15 | ## The Problem: Your Release Process is Bleeding Hours You Can't Get Back
16 | 
17 | Picture a typical Friday afternoon production incident. Something broke in the last deployment. The on-call engineer needs to find the approved runbook, the change-approval record, the test evidence, and the audit log of who touched the config file — and needs them *now*.

19 | Here's what actually happens:

21 | - The "official" document is in **FileNet** — but which version? Nobody knows which one was signed off.
22 | - The working copy the team actually used is on a **shared drive** — also in three different folders with three different names.
23 | - The change approval lives in an **email thread** from six months ago that nobody has bookmarked.
24 | - The mainframe-attached DMS the infrastructure team uses hasn't been integrated with anything, ever, because nobody wants to touch it.
25 | - The audit tracker is a **spreadsheet** updated manually, sometimes.
26 | 
27 | That's five systems that don't talk to each other, and the clock is ticking.
28 | 
29 | **This is not an edge case.** It is the default state for every organization running enterprise-grade workloads — IBM i shops, IBM Z shops, banks, insurers, government agencies — any place where the document estate spans legacy and modern systems simultaneously. And it generates a measurable, recurring tax:

33 | | **Incident reconstruction** | 2–4 hours per incident reconstructing who approved what, across which system, at what version |
34 | | **Approval archaeology** | Days of work per compliance audit to prove change-approval trails that should be instant lookups |
35 | | **Version confusion** | Runbooks and deployment checklists exist in 3–5 near-duplicate copies; nobody can tell which is authoritative |
36 | | **Approval-by-email** | Sign-offs that exist only in an inbox — unfindable 6 months later when an auditor asks |
37 | | **Migration paralysis** | Teams want unified governance but cannot afford to move 10 years of content out of FileNet or off a mainframe |
38 | 
39 | **C-ECM removes this tax — without a migration.**
40 |

42 | 
43 | ## The Solution: One Governance Layer Over Every System You Already Have
44 | 
45 | C-ECM is a governance and intelligence layer that sits *in front of* whatever storage each team already uses — IBM FileNet, IBM i (AS/400), IBM Z mainframe, Alfresco, SharePoint, Google Drive, Box, S3, Azure Blob, IBM Cloud Object Storage, local disk — and gives every one of those systems the same approval gates, the same immutable audit trail, and the same cross-repository search, on day one, with zero files moved and zero migrations required.
46 | 
47 | It looks like a shared drive. It feels like a shared drive. But every action behind the scenes is now:
48 | 
49 | - **Approval-gated** — documents flow through defined, multi-step, quorum-based sign-off workflows before they can be published or finalized
50 | - **Version-controlled** — every upload creates an immutable version; check-out/check-in prevents silent overwrites with a server-enforced soft lock
51 | - **Audit-logged** — every login, view, edit, approval, rejection, and deletion is captured in a tamper-evident log with user, timestamp, and action type

79 |        │                      │                      │

81 |   ─────────────         ─────────              ────────────────

85 |   webhook_service                               workflows, locks,

87 |        │

97 | ### Event Bus: the secret to a unified audit trail
98 | 
99 | Every write to any backend — upload, rename, delete, approval vote, version restore — flows through one choke point: `activity_service.record_event()`. That single call fans out synchronously to:
100 | 
101 | 1. **The audit log** (SQLite, append-only, WAL mode)
102 | 2. **In-app notifications** (per-user notification store)
103 | 3. **Outbound webhooks** (HMAC-SHA256 signed, SSRF-hardened)
104 | 
105 | No provider has to know the audit log exists. No new provider needs new audit code. The observer/event-bus pattern is what makes a unified, tamper-resistant trail possible across 11 unrelated storage systems.

107 | ### Design Patterns in Play
108 | 
109 | | Pattern | Where | Why |
110 | |---|---|---|
111 | | **Strategy / Adapter** | `StorageProvider` ABC + 11 concrete backends | IBM Z and Google Drive expose identical interfaces to the rest of the app |
112 | | **Observer / Event Bus** | `activity_service` | One `record_event()` call reaches audit, notifications, and webhooks; adding a subscriber never touches provider code |
113 | | **Repository** | `*_store.py` per domain | Routers never write raw SQL; data access is encapsulated and testable |
114 | | **State Machine** | Approval workflow engine | Instances move through validated transitions only (`pending → in_review → approved / rejected / cancelled`) with per-step quorum |
115 | | **Factory / Registry** | `get_provider(key)` in `registry.py` | Self-registers every backend; verified thread-safe under concurrent first access |
116 | | **Layered Architecture** | Presentation → API → Domain → Data → Providers | A UI change or storage-backend swap never leaks across layers |
